module: Algorithms and Data Structures Using Java

questions.q: A Java array contains 12 elements. What is the largest valid index?
questions.e: Java arrays use zero-based indexing, so the final index is length minus one.

questions.q: An algorithm checks every pair of distinct elements once using i<j. How many pairs are checked for n elements?
questions.e: There are n choices for the first position and n−1 later positions, divided by two because each unordered pair is counted once.

questions.q: A method performs one loop over n items and a separate nested loop over n items. What is its overall time complexity?
questions.e: The costs O(n) and O(n²) add; the dominant term is O(n²).

questions.q: Which statement about Big-O notation is correct?
o: It gives an exact runtime in seconds
It describes an asymptotic upper bound
It applies only to recursive algorithms
questions.e: Big-O expresses an asymptotic upper bound on growth, independent of machine-specific seconds.

questions.q: An algorithm uses an auxiliary array whose size grows proportionally to n. What is its auxiliary space complexity?
questions.e: An additional array with a linear number of entries requires linear auxiliary space.

questions.q: A loop variable is multiplied by 3 after every iteration until it exceeds n. How many iterations occur?
questions.e: The variable grows geometrically, so the number of multiplications is logarithmic in n.

questions.q: A method makes two recursive calls on n/2 elements and then merges their results in linear time. Which recurrence models it?
questions.e: Two half-size recursive calls plus a linear merge produce this recurrence.

questions.q: Which ADT property describes what operations are available without specifying their implementation?
questions.e: An ADT specifies values and permitted operations while hiding implementation details.

questions.q: For an array-backed list, why is accessing element at index i typically O(1)?
o: It computes the element address from the base address and index
questions.e: Contiguous storage permits direct address calculation from the index.

questions.q: A sorted array has 40 elements. How many elements must shift in the worst case when inserting at index 0?
questions.e: All existing 40 elements? For an array of size 40, inserting at index 0 shifts 40 elements; answer should be 40.

questions.q: A stack receives push(4), push(9), pop(), push(2), pop(). What value is returned by the second pop?
questions.e: After the first pop removes 9, pushing 2 makes 2 the top; the next pop returns 2.

questions.q: A stack is implemented using a singly linked list with the head as top. What is the time complexity of push?
questions.e: Insertion at the head updates a constant number of references.

questions.q: A queue is implemented with a linked list that stores both front and rear references. What is enqueue complexity?
questions.e: The rear reference permits direct insertion at the tail.

questions.q: A circular queue has capacity 8 and uses one unused slot to distinguish full from empty. What is its maximum number of stored elements?
questions.e: One slot remains unused, so usable capacity is array capacity minus one.

questions.q: In a circular queue of capacity m, how is the next rear index commonly calculated?
questions.e: Modulo m wraps the index from the final array position back to zero.

questions.q: A deque supports insertion and deletion at both ends. Which operation is not inherently supported by a deque?
o: Remove the middle element in O(1)
questions.e: A deque exposes both ends; arbitrary middle removal is not a constant-time end operation.

questions.q: A priority queue removes the item with the smallest key first. Which heap is a natural implementation?
questions.e: A min-heap keeps the smallest key at the root for efficient minimum removal.

questions.q: When a binary min-heap inserts a new key, where is it initially placed?
o: At the next available leaf position
questions.e: Insertion preserves the complete-tree shape by filling the next available leaf before sifting upward.

questions.q: In a binary heap stored in a zero-based array, what is the right child index of node i?
questions.e: For zero-based heap indexing, left child is 2i+1 and right child is 2i+2.

questions.q: A max-heap array is [50, 30, 40, 10, 20]. After removing the maximum, which value is moved to the root before heapifying?
questions.e: The last element, 10, replaces the root before sift-down restores the heap property.

questions.q: In a singly linked list, what must be updated when inserting a node at the head?
o: Only the new node's next and the head reference
questions.e: The new node points to the former head, then head is updated to the new node.

questions.q: A singly linked list has no tail reference. What is the worst-case time to append a node?
questions.e: Without a tail reference, traversal is needed to find the final node.

questions.q: Which advantage does a doubly linked list provide over a singly linked list?
questions.e: Each node has previous and next references, enabling traversal in both directions.

questions.q: In a circular singly linked list with at least one node, what does the last node's next reference point to?
questions.e: The last node links back to the head, forming a cycle.

questions.q: A pointer/reference to node X is available in a singly linked list. Which deletion can be done in O(1) without access to the previous node, assuming X is not the tail?
o: Delete X by copying its successor's data and bypassing successor
questions.e: Copy the next node's data into X and bypass that next node; this cannot delete the tail this way.

questions.q: Which condition detects the end of a normal singly linked list traversal?
questions.e: A non-circular list terminates when the current reference becomes null.

questions.q: Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm is commonly used to detect what?
o: A cycle in a linked list
A duplicate in a sorted array only
questions.e: Two references moving at different speeds meet if a cycle exists.

questions.q: For a singly linked list, what is the time complexity of finding the middle using slow and fast references?
o: O(log n) time and O(n) space
questions.e: The fast reference advances twice as quickly, so both traverse the list in linear time with constant extra space.

questions.q: Which operation on a singly linked list requires a predecessor reference to unlink a known node in the usual implementation?
questions.e: To unlink a node, the predecessor's next reference must bypass it.

questions.q: What is the main structural difference between a circular linked list and a linear linked list?
o: The last node links back to the first node
Every circular list is doubly linked
questions.e: A circular list connects its final node back to the first rather than ending with null.

questions.q: What is the result of factorial(4) when factorial(n) returns 1 for n<=1 and otherwise n*factorial(n−1)?
questions.e: The calls evaluate 4×3×2×1, which equals 24.

questions.q: A recursive method makes exactly one call with n−1 until n reaches zero. What is its recursion depth for input n, excluding constant framing calls?
questions.e: There are linearly many nested calls before reaching the base case.

questions.q: Which risk is most directly associated with recursion on a very large input in Java?
questions.e: Each active recursive call consumes stack space; excessive depth can exhaust the thread stack.

questions.q: A recursive binary search halves the interval at each call. What is its maximum recursion depth?
questions.e: The search range is halved on every call, yielding logarithmic depth.

questions.q: Which change converts a recursive factorial into an accumulator-based tail-recursive form?
o: Multiply after the recursive call returns
Pass the accumulated product into the next call
Create a new array per call
questions.e: The accumulated result is passed as an argument so no computation remains after the recursive call.

questions.q: For the recurrence T(n)=T(n−1)+O(1), what is the asymptotic time complexity?
questions.e: The recurrence adds constant work across n levels.

questions.q: A recursive function branches into three calls of size n/2 and does O(n) extra work. Which recurrence represents it?
questions.e: Three recursive subproblems of half size plus linear non-recursive work give this recurrence.

questions.q: Why is a base case essential in a recursive algorithm?
o: It guarantees termination for valid input paths
questions.e: A reachable base case stops recursive calls and prevents unbounded recursion.

questions.q: A recursive method returns f(n−1)+f(n−2) with constant base cases. What is a typical issue with its naive implementation?
o: It recomputes the same subproblems many times
questions.e: The recursion tree contains overlapping subproblems, causing repeated work.

questions.q: Which technique stores results of solved recursive subproblems to avoid recomputation?
questions.e: Memoization caches previously computed results and reuses them when the same state recurs.

questions.q: In a binary tree, what is the maximum number of nodes at level L when the root is level 0?
questions.e: A binary tree can double the number of nodes at each successive level.

questions.q: A full binary tree has 7 internal nodes. How many leaves does it have?
questions.e: In a full binary tree, the number of leaves equals internal nodes plus one.

questions.q: Which traversal visits the root between the left and right subtrees?
questions.e: Inorder traversal follows left subtree, root, then right subtree.

questions.q: Which traversal is most directly implemented using a queue?
questions.e: Breadth-first level-order traversal uses a queue to process nodes in discovery order.

questions.q: What is the height of a tree consisting of only one node when height is measured in edges?
questions.e: A single-node tree has no edges on its longest root-to-leaf path.

questions.q: Which property defines a binary search tree with distinct keys?
o: Left subtree keys are smaller and right subtree keys are larger
All leaves are at the same level
questions.e: BST ordering places smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right subtree.

questions.q: What is the worst-case search time in a completely skewed binary search tree with n nodes?
questions.e: A skewed BST behaves like a linked list, requiring linear traversal in the worst case.

questions.q: Which data structure is typically used for iterative depth-first traversal of a binary tree?
questions.e: A stack stores pending nodes for depth-first traversal.

questions.q: A BST's inorder traversal produces 2, 5, 8, 11. What can be concluded if keys are distinct?
o: The tree contains exactly four levels
The keys are visited in sorted order
questions.e: Inorder traversal of a BST visits keys in ascending order.

questions.q: Which tree traversal is useful for deleting a tree because children are processed before their parent?
questions.e: Postorder processes left and right subtrees before the current node.

questions.q: Binary search is applied to a sorted array of 256 elements. Approximately how many halvings reduce the interval to one element?
questions.e: Since 256=2^8, eight halvings reduce the range to one.

questions.q: When a sorted array contains duplicate target values, which binary-search modification finds the first occurrence?
o: Continue searching the left half after equality
Continue searching the right half after equality
questions.e: After finding equality, save the index and continue left to locate an earlier occurrence.

questions.q: What is the worst-case comparison complexity of linear search in an array of n items?
questions.e: The target may be absent or at the final position, requiring all n items to be examined.

questions.q: Which condition must hold for standard binary search on an array?
o: Elements must be sorted according to the searched order
Array length must be a power of two
questions.e: Binary search relies on sorted order to discard half of the remaining range.

questions.q: A binary search uses mid=(low+high)/2 with large positive integer indices. What is a safer Java expression to avoid possible addition overflow?
questions.e: Computing the difference first avoids overflowing the sum of two large indices.

questions.q: A lower-bound search returns the first index whose value is greater than or equal to target. If no such value exists, what should it return?
questions.e: The insertion position after all n elements is n when every value is smaller than target.

questions.q: What does interpolation search use to estimate the likely position of a key?
o: The key's value relative to endpoint values
questions.e: Interpolation estimates a position from the target's relative value between the low and high endpoints.

questions.q: Which search is generally preferable for a linked list with no random access?
questions.e: A linked list cannot efficiently access a middle node by index, so sequential search is appropriate.

questions.q: In binary search over [low, high] inclusive, when target is greater than arr[mid], what is the next low value?
questions.e: The middle item is already known to be too small, so the remaining interval begins at mid+1.

questions.q: A search algorithm checks the middle, then quarters, then eighths of the range. Which growth rate best describes the number of checks?
questions.e: Repeatedly reducing the remaining range by a constant factor produces logarithmic search time.

questions.q: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly selects the minimum remaining element and places it at the next sorted position?
questions.e: Selection sort selects the smallest item from the unsorted suffix for each position.

questions.q: For insertion sort, what is the best-case time complexity on an already sorted array?
questions.e: Each item is compared with its predecessor and no shifting is needed, producing linear time.

questions.q: Which sorting algorithm is stable in its standard implementation?
questions.e: A stable merge procedure takes equal keys from the left run first, preserving their relative order.

questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort when each partition places one item on one side and n−1 on the other?
questions.e: Highly unbalanced partitions produce a recursion chain with quadratic total partition work.

questions.q: What is the typical auxiliary space complexity of recursive merge sort on an array?
questions.e: The merge process uses temporary storage proportional to the number of array elements.

questions.q: Which sorting algorithm has O(n log n) worst-case time and can sort an array in place with O(1) auxiliary storage?
questions.e: Heap sort provides O(n log n) worst-case time and can be implemented in-place.

questions.q: In bubble sort, what does one complete left-to-right pass guarantee for ascending order?
o: The largest unsorted element reaches its final position
questions.e: Adjacent swaps move the largest element of the unsorted portion to its rightmost position.

questions.q: Why does counting sort not fit the comparison-sort lower bound of Ω(n log n)?
o: It sorts by counting occurrences in a bounded key range rather than comparing pairs
questions.e: Counting sort exploits integer key ranges and does not rely solely on pairwise comparisons.

questions.q: A stable sort is applied to records with equal keys. What must it preserve?
o: The records' insertion time in the CPU
The order of unequal keys only
questions.e: Stability preserves the original relative order of records whose sort keys are equal.

questions.q: For an array of n elements, how many passes does standard selection sort perform in its usual form?
questions.e: Each pass places one element, leaving the final element already in position after n−1 passes.

questions.q: A hash table uses separate chaining. What happens when two keys hash to the same bucket?
o: Both entries are stored in that bucket's chain
questions.e: Separate chaining stores colliding entries together in a bucket collection such as a linked list.

questions.q: In open addressing, what does linear probing do after a collision?
o: Checks the next slot in sequence
Rehashes the entire key as a string
Moves the key to the root
questions.e: Linear probing examines successive table positions until an available slot or matching key is found.

questions.q: A hash table's load factor is defined as which ratio?
o: Table capacity divided by number of entries
Number of entries divided by table capacity
Number of collisions divided by entries
questions.e: Load factor α=n/m is the number of stored entries divided by the number of slots.

questions.q: Why can deletion be tricky in an open-addressed hash table?
o: A cleared slot may incorrectly terminate later searches along a probe sequence
questions.e: A search must continue past a deleted slot; tombstones preserve the probe chain.

questions.q: Which property is desirable for a hash function used in a hash table?
o: It maps every key to a unique index
It distributes expected keys uniformly across buckets
questions.e: Uniform distribution reduces collisions and helps maintain expected constant-time operations.

questions.q: If a hash table doubles its capacity and reinserts all entries, why must entries be rehashed?
o: Bucket positions depend on the table capacity
questions.e: The bucket index is typically computed using the new capacity, so old positions may no longer be valid.

questions.q: What is the expected search time in a well-distributed hash table with a controlled load factor?
questions.e: With a suitable hash function and bounded load factor, expected lookup examines a constant number of entries.

questions.q: Which collision strategy stores multiple values in a collection associated with each bucket?
questions.e: Separate chaining keeps colliding keys in a bucket-level collection.

questions.q: In double hashing, how is the next probe position determined?
o: By adding a second hash-derived step size
By always moving exactly one slot
questions.e: A second hash function supplies the probe step, reducing primary clustering.

questions.q: What is primary clustering associated with in open addressing?
o: Long contiguous runs of occupied slots that attract further probes
Duplicate values in a linked list
questions.e: Linear probing can form contiguous occupied runs, increasing probe lengths.

questions.q: In an unweighted graph, which algorithm finds shortest paths measured by number of edges from a source?
questions.e: BFS explores vertices level by level, so first discovery gives the minimum edge count.

questions.q: Which data structure is central to a standard BFS implementation?
questions.e: A FIFO queue processes discovered vertices in increasing distance order.

questions.q: Which data structure is commonly used by iterative DFS?
questions.e: DFS uses a stack, explicitly or through the call stack, to explore a path deeply.

questions.q: For an adjacency-list graph, what is the time complexity of BFS over all reachable vertices and edges?
questions.e: Each vertex is visited once and each adjacency-list edge is examined a constant number of times.

questions.q: Dijkstra's algorithm is appropriate under which edge-weight condition?
o: All edges must have negative weights
Every edge must have weight one
The graph must be a tree
questions.e: Dijkstra's greedy finalization is correct when no edge has a negative weight.

questions.q: Which algorithm can compute single-source shortest paths in a graph with negative edges and detect reachable negative cycles?
questions.e: Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges repeatedly and uses an extra pass to detect reachable negative cycles.

questions.q: What does Floyd-Warshall compute?
questions.e: Floyd-Warshall updates shortest distances for every ordered pair of vertices.

questions.q: A directed acyclic graph is commonly abbreviated as what?
questions.e: DAG stands for directed acyclic graph.

questions.q: Which algorithmic process produces a topological ordering of a DAG using indegrees and a queue?
questions.e: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes zero-indegree vertices and updates neighbouring indegrees.

questions.q: A graph has V vertices and E edges. What is the space complexity of an adjacency matrix?
questions.e: An adjacency matrix reserves one cell for each possible ordered vertex pair.

questions.q: Which technique solves a problem by combining solutions to independent smaller subproblems?
questions.e: Divide and conquer divides the input, solves subproblems, and combines their results.

questions.q: Merge sort is an example of which algorithm design technique?
questions.e: Merge sort recursively divides the array and merges sorted halves.

questions.q: Dynamic programming is especially useful when a problem has which pair of properties?
questions.e: DP reuses solutions to overlapping subproblems and relies on optimal substructure.

questions.q: What is the main distinction between memoization and tabulation?
o: Memoization is top-down; tabulation is bottom-up
They are unrelated to dynamic programming
questions.e: Memoization caches results during recursive evaluation, while tabulation fills a table iteratively.

questions.q: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step. What must be established to guarantee global optimality?
o: A greedy-choice property and appropriate optimal substructure
questions.e: A proof must show that a locally optimal choice can be part of a globally optimal solution.

questions.q: Which technique explores candidate solutions and abandons a partial candidate when it cannot lead to a valid solution?
questions.e: Backtracking prunes a search branch when its partial assignment violates constraints.

questions.q: What does amortized analysis measure?
o: Average cost per operation over a sequence, with a worst-case guarantee for the sequence
questions.e: Amortized analysis bounds total sequence cost and spreads occasional expensive operations across operations.

questions.q: An operation costs O(n) occasionally but O(1) for most appends in a geometrically resizing array. What is the amortized append cost?
questions.e: Geometric growth makes the total copying work over n appends linear, yielding constant amortized cost.

questions.q: Which statement about best-case and worst-case complexity is correct?
o: Worst case considers the most expensive input of a given size
Best case is the average of all inputs
Worst case depends only on programming language
questions.e: Worst-case analysis bounds the maximum cost among inputs of a specified size.

questions.q: An algorithm uses a constant number of variables and no input-sized auxiliary structure. What is its auxiliary space complexity?
questions.e: A fixed amount of extra storage does not grow with input size.
